brief: Tonight is Push A — chest, shoulders, triceps — and it is your fourth training day in a row. That is the fact shaping the card, so almost nothing on it goes up. Every single weight tonight is one you have already lifted; there is no new number anywhere. First, your question, because you asked it in writing and it deserves an answer before anything else. Under the leg curls on Sunday you wrote: four sets on the same day as RDLs, too many hamstrings or just right? Just right — keep the four. You took all four at 142.5 for twelve, twelve, twelve and twelve, which is the top of what that slot asks, and nothing fell off across the four. Hamstrings that were overcooked would have shown it in that fourth set, and yours did not. The one set that did go missing that night was the fourth RDL — and the RDL runs first on the card, so the curls that come after it cannot have taken it. Two of the three trainers wrote that answer independently, off the same log. It is not a card on your plan screen, and you should know why: the app will only show you a Yes/No card for something that would actually change the program, and 'keep the four' changes nothing, so there is nothing to tap. This paragraph and the notice at the top of your screen are the answer. If they are still sore two days out, write that in a note and it goes to three. Now tonight. Smith incline press runs all four sets at 175 instead of opening at 165. Your reps climbed last time — 165 for six, then 175 for six, seven and eight — so the opener was lighter than the weight you finished on and it was not testing you. Same top weight, one more honest exposure at it, and the job is eight on every set before it moves. Dumbbell shoulder press starts at the 40s for all three. You got ten on the 35s, which is the top of that range, and then pressed the 40s for nine twice. The 35s have done their job and there is no dumbbell between them and the 40s. Nine on the first set is a fine night; ten is the target. Three things come down. Overhead cable triceps is two sets tonight, not three — 53.75 then 55. On both Push days in your log the third set is the one that dies: twelve, eleven, nine on the 14th, and eleven, eleven, ten on the 3rd. Two honest sets beat three where the last one is a fade. Rope pushdown drops a pin on the back two sets: 52.5, then 47.5 and 47.5. This one is not you being tired — it is a weight left over from the old rep range. You accepted widening this lift to twelve-to-fifteen reps on the 14th, the same night that session was logged, so tonight is the first Push A it has ever run on, and 52.5 was set when the ask was ten-to-twelve. Fourteen, eleven and ten under a twelve-rep floor is a weight that has not caught up with its own range yet. Cable lateral raise keeps three sets but the last one drops one micro plate to 8.75, because thirteen, thirteen, then ten is a third set finishing under the floor rather than a weight problem on the first two. Chest press, cable crossover and reverse pec deck all stay exactly where they are — both trainers agreed, and none of the three has earned a move yet. Chase the top of the range on each. Three things you should know that are not numbers. Yesterday morning's review did not run — no packet was written on the 16th. Your Legs B card was still correct, because Sunday's packet was written for Legs B and that is the session you did, but the review itself missed a day and you should hear that from me rather than assume it ran. Second, on two of your three shoulder press sets last Push day the set was logged within a few seconds of the rest bell, which makes it impossible to tell from the log how long you actually rested. Not an accusation — I genuinely cannot read it. If you are cutting rest short there, it will show up as a bad set before it shows up as anything else. Third, the last exercise of your session keeps getting eaten: two sets instead of three on the 3rd, the 14th and again on Sunday. Whatever is last in the order is systematically paying for it, and right now that is your rear delts. There are two cards on your plan screen about exactly that — one adds a third rear-delt set on Push A, the other moves that lift out of last place so the extra set is not just more work at the end of a long night. Take them together or not at all. Last, and good: you weighed in on Sunday. 206, the same as 21 July — twenty-six days, no change. That is the first new reading in nearly a month and it is worth more to March than any weight on tonight's card. Meso 1 closes on 23 August, Meso 2 opens on the 24th, and there is no back-off week in between.

flags.note: Tonight is your fourth training day in a row. Every weight on the card is one you have already lifted — nothing new goes on the bar.
Your leg-curl question, answered: keep the four sets. All four went 142.5 for twelve on Sunday with nothing falling off, and the set that went missing was the fourth RDL, which runs before them.
Yesterday's review did not run — no packet was written on 16 August. Your Legs B numbers were still right, because Sunday's packet was written for Legs B, but the review missed a day.
Overhead cable triceps is two sets tonight instead of three: the third set has finished at or under the floor on both Push days in your log.
The last exercise of your session has come in two sets instead of three on 3, 14 and 16 August — whatever runs last is paying for it, and right now that is your rear delts.
On two of three shoulder press sets last Push day the set was logged within seconds of the rest bell, so how long you actually rested cannot be read from the log.
Meso 1 closes on 23 August and Meso 2 opens on the 24th. There is no back-off week in between.
You weighed in on Sunday: 206, the same as 21 July. First new reading in twenty-six days.

proposals.why: Face pulls have now come off all four of your days, so the back of your shoulder is down to five sets in the whole week and only two of them are on Push A — a night that carries thirteen sets of chest and front-shoulder work — and on 14 August you took both of those two at 90 for twelve without dropping a rep, so this makes Push A three sets, the same three you already do on Push B.

This is the other half of the card above, and they only work together: your last exercise has come in short on 3, 14 and 16 August, and on Push A the lift sitting last is the reverse pec deck, so adding a third set without moving it just puts more work in the spot that already gets eaten — this runs it fifth, straight after the shoulder press and ahead of the triceps and lateral raises, so your rear delts get a fresh slot instead of the dregs.

You accepted exactly this change on Legs B yesterday and Legs A still has the old ceiling on it — the hanging leg raise carries no weight, so reps are the only thing about it that can grow, and on both 26 July and 2 August your first two Legs A sets finished at twelve, which is the top of what that slot asks, so it is frozen there and can never ask for more; twelve to fifteen makes twelve the floor instead of the ceiling on both leg days.

overrides.reason: All four sets at 175 instead of opening at 165. Last Push day your reps climbed as the night went on — 165 for six, then 175 for six, seven and eight — which means the opener was lighter than the weight you finished on and was not testing you. Same top weight as last time, one more exposure at it. Eight on every set is the job before it moves again. The recovery trainer wanted this left exactly as it was on a fourth straight day; it lost, because its own reason said nothing here is worn out.

The 40s for all three sets. You got ten on the 35s last Push day, which is the top of the range, and then pressed the 40s for nine twice — so 40 is a weight you have already worked, and there is no dumbbell on the rack between 35 and 40. Nine on the first set is a fine night; ten is the target. One thing I cannot read: on two of those three sets you logged within a few seconds of the rest bell, so I have no idea how long you actually rested there.

Two sets tonight, not three: 53.75 then 55. The third set is the one that keeps dying — twelve, eleven, nine on the 14th, and eleven, eleven, ten on the 3rd — so it fails on a fresh day and on a tired one alike. Both weights are ones you have already handled. The trainers split: one wanted three sets with the 55 taken off, the other wanted the weights left alone and the third set dropped. The set came off, because two Push days say it is the set, not the pin.

Three sets still, but the last one drops one micro plate to 8.75. You went thirteen, thirteen, then ten at a flat 10 — the first two were fine and the third finished under the twelve-rep floor, so this is a last-set problem, not a weight problem. The recovery trainer wanted the third set gone entirely; it lost, because dropping 1.25 pounds is a cheaper fix than deleting a shoulder set seven months out from a show.

52.5, then 47.5 and 47.5. Read this one carefully, because it is not what it looks like: you accepted widening this lift to twelve-to-fifteen reps on 14 August, the same night that session was logged, so tonight is the first Push A the new range has ever run on. The 52.5 was set when the ask was ten-to-twelve. Fourteen, eleven and ten under a twelve-rep floor is a weight that has not caught up with its own range yet, not a lift you are too tired for. The recovery trainer voted to skip this entirely on fatigue grounds and I overruled it — that is allowed on fatigue, it would not be on pain. It got the triceps set above instead.

dissent.progression: All four sets at 175 — his reps climbed 6, 7, 8 at that weight, so the 165 opener is lighter than what he finished on.
dissent.recovery: Hold it exactly as it was, because tonight is the fourth training day in a row.
dissent.why: Progression. Recovery's argument here is the calendar, not the lift, and its own reason concedes that nothing on this exercise is worn out — reps that climb across a session are the signature of a man warming up, not one running out. This is also not a load increase: 175 is the weight he finished on last time, and all this does is stop wasting his first set on a weight he has already passed. I gave recovery its fourth-day argument where it has lift-specific evidence to back it, on the triceps below. Here it had none.

dissent.progression: Start at the 40s for all three — he hit the top of the range on the 35s and already pressed the 40s for nine twice.
dissent.recovery: Hold at 35, 40, 40 on a fourth straight day, with a caution that the rest timings on two sets cannot be read.
dissent.why: Progression, and only just. The 35s gave him ten, which is the top of what the slot asks, and the dumbbell rack has nothing between 35 and 40 — so the choice was 40 or handing him back a weight he has finished with. He has already pressed the 40s for nine, so this is not a weight he has never moved; it asks for one more rep on a bell he owns. Recovery's rest-data caution is real and I have put it in front of him as a flag rather than quietly pricing it into the numbers, because it is a question only he can answer.

dissent.progression: Three sets, all at 53.75 — the 55 comes off because set three fell to nine, under the floor.
dissent.recovery: Two sets instead of three, weights untouched — the third set is the one that keeps arriving already tired.
dissent.why: Recovery, and this is the seat's strongest evidence of the night. Progression read one bad set as one bad pin, but 3 August refutes that: three flat sets at 55 there gave eleven, eleven and ten, all inside the range, so 55 is not too heavy. What both sessions actually share is that the THIRD set is the weakest one — nine on the 14th, ten on the 3rd. That is a position problem, not a load problem, and cutting the position is the honest fix. It is also the concession that earns me the right to overrule recovery's veto on the rope pushdown: it asked for load off a fourth straight day, and this is load off, taken from the place its own evidence points at.

dissent.progression: Keep three sets, drop the last one to 8.75 so it finishes inside the range instead of dying short.
dissent.recovery: Two sets instead of three — the third lost a quarter of its reps.
dissent.why: Progression. Both seats saw the same thing, a third set coming in at ten under a twelve-rep floor, and proposed opposite fixes. Recovery's costs a whole shoulder set; progression's costs 1.25 pounds. Side delts are a front-line muscle for a March stage and he is already losing rear-delt sets to the end of the session — I am not spending another shoulder set to solve a problem that one micro plate solves. If 8.75 also finishes short next Push day, then it is fatigue and recovery was right, and the set comes off then.

dissent.progression: 52.5 then 47.5 twice — the back two sets missed the twelve-rep floor, so they drop one pin.
dissent.recovery: Skip it entirely tonight, plus a formal veto on fatigue grounds: second triceps lift, fourth straight day, no deload until after 23 August.
dissent.why: Progression, and I am overruling a veto to do it — which the rules allow on fatigue grounds and would forbid outright on pain or injury. The deciding fact is one neither number seat had in full and the program trainer supplied: he accepted widening this lift to twelve-to-fifteen reps on 14 August, the same night that session was logged. The 52.5 on the card was set for a ten-to-twelve ask. So fourteen, eleven and ten is not a tired man failing a floor — it is a weight that has never once run under its own new range, and tonight is the first Push A where it does. Skipping the lift would delete the first real test of a change he already approved. Recovery is not wrong that day four needs something taken off it; I took it off the overhead triceps instead, where two sessions of evidence pointed.
